newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-All-male Christian revivalism sweeps America.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-All-male Christian revivalism sweeps America.

text.p: In a domed stadium usually used by the Detroit Lions football team, an all-male crowd of 57,000 sings hymns, listens to sermons, confesses sins, holds hands, sheds tears and is "born again" for Jesus.

It is a two-day meeting of the Promise Keepers, the fastest-growing Christian revivalist movement to sweep America in recent times that last year mobilised 1.1 million men to gather in 22 sports stadiums nationwide for 14 hours of preaching and prayers.

Begun in 1990 by Bill McCartney, a former football coach at the University of Colorado, Promise Keepers has grown like wildfire with its Christian evangelist message asking men to return to Jesus and take charge of their families.

This year, in addition to 21 stadium weekends, of which the Pontiac gathering was the first, the group is planning its biggest event ever -- a national rally and day of prayer in Washington on Oct. 4, which may outdo the 1995 "Million Man March" of black men convened in Washington by controversial Moslem preacher Louis Farrakhan.

"Men will kneel in humility and rise in unity. We're asking God to come in His manifest presence so the church of Jesus Christ will be forever changed," said Dale Schlafer, vice president for revival and awakening.
The group now employs a staff of 452, 40 percent of them women, and has a projected 1997 budget of $117 million.
Its most controversial message, articulated by some preachers at Promise Keepers events, is for men to take back "Christian leadership" of their families.
MEN BE SENSITIVE

Dallas preacher Tony Evans put it bluntly at one early Promise Keepers event: "There can be no compromise here. If you're going to lead, you must lead. Be sensitive. Listen. Treat the lady gently and lovingly. But lead."

A Promise Keepers event can be a heady experience. Men, mostly but not exclusively white, sway and sing. They kneel and lift their arms to heaven. They cry and hug and they swear to return to God and become better fathers and husbands. Hundreds come forward to the altar to be "born again" and accept Jesus as their personal saviour.

"They say we'll never treat women with respect, never swallow our pride, never come together, never love each other. In Jesus Christ it will be done, because he will do it," blares a video shown at the start of the event.
"Tonight, this stadium becomes a sanctuary and we, longing to be Godly men, worship our king."

Promise Keepers commit themselves to keeping seven pledges: to honour and worship Jesus; to pursue "vital relationships" with other men; to practice spiritual, moral, ethical and sexual purity; to build strong marriages and families through love, protection and biblical values; to support their church; to reach out across racial and denominational barriers; and to spread Christianity.

Recently, the organisation appears to be trying to tone down its male supremacy message a little. A recent article in the Promise Keepers magazine by preacher Gary Smalley of Branson, Missouri, said a man should view his wife as "the most important player on the team ... She is equally capable of calling the plays. That means not only encouraging her to have a say in running the team, but to listen to her viewpoint and try the plays she calls."
SOME WOMEN NOT IMPRESED
But Rosemary Dempsey, national action vice president for the National Organisation for Women, is not impressed.

"The rhetoric may have been toned down but the basic message is that men have lost or been pushed out of family leadership and they have to take back that leadership or the Christian family is going down the toilet," she said.
"This is a huge, very right-wing movement that is intent on reversing what the women's movement has accomplished using very powerful psychological techniques," said Dempsey.

Jim Wallis, of Call to Renewal, a group that works for Christian dialogue and social action, said Promise Keepers was responding to a deep need among men confused by their role in modern American society.
"Anyone saying anything about male spirituality and about men taking responsibility fills a vacuum," he said.

But Wallis said Promise Keepers had still not answered a central question: "Are they saying that for men to step forward, women must step backward back to the kitchen? They have not answered that yet."
